short: The winter campaigns that ended Kievan Rus' and subjected its princes for two centuries.
full:
Batu Khan's army crossed the Volga in late 1237 and took Ryazan in December after a five-day siege. The Mongols campaigned in winter, using frozen rivers as roads, which is precisely when the forest principalities expected to be safe. Vladimir fell in February 1238 and Grand Prince Yuri II was killed on the Sit River; the little town of Kozelsk held out for seven weeks and was destroyed for it. Novgorod escaped, saved by the spring thaw and the swamps.

The southern principalities were taken in 1239 and 1240. Kiev, the mother of Rus' cities, was stormed on 6 December 1240 after the walls were breached near the Lech gates; the papal envoy Giovanni da Pian del Carpine rode through six years later and counted two hundred houses standing among the bones. Galicia-Volhynia submitted, and Batu's columns pressed on into Poland and Hungary. The surviving princes travelled to Sarai for patents to rule, and paid tribute until 1480.
